blocks.content: Two fundamentally different ways of thinking about code. One organises the world around functions and data transformations. The other organises it around objects and their behaviour. Knowing when to use which and why is what separates a senior engineer from a junior one.
1. The core
Imagine you're building a system that processes orders. Here's the same problem through two completely different lenses.
FUNCTIONAL DESIGN (FD)
"What transformations does data go through?"

You think in pipelines. Data flows in, gets transformed by pure functions, flows out. No objects, no state hidden inside classes. Everything is explicit you can trace exactly what changed, when, and why.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/2aef6e09-8e79-44a7-8706-90925d086b4f.png
The world is: input → function → output. Functions don't remember anything between calls.
OBJECT-ORIENTED DESIGN (OOD)
"What entities exist and what can they do?"
blocks.text: "What entities exist and what can they do?"

blocks.content: You think in objects. Each object bundles its data and the methods that operate on it. Objects hold state, communicate with each other, and model real-world concepts directly.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/dd659e7b-a340-4ccb-b957-9b5c0ad3d190.png
The world is: objects with identity, state, and behaviour.
2. How each one thinks about the same concepts
blocks.text: 2. How each one thinks about the same concepts

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512618122-682357259.png

3. Same feature, two implementations
Let's apply a discount to an order. See how differently each paradigm approaches the exact same task.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512620211-194870250.png
blocks.alt: Diagram showing where the discount logic lives, a separate pure function returning a new Order versus a method inside Order that mutates it in place

blocks.content: FUNCTIONAL APPROACH
Data and logic are separate. The function takes an order in and returns a new order out it never modifies the original.
OOP APPROACH
The Order object owns its own discount logic. It knows its items and can apply a discount to itself.

codes.python:
class Order:
    def __init__(self, total: float):
        # Private attribute to protect data
        self._total = total

    def apply_discount(self, percent: float) -> None:
        # Update existing total directly
        self._total = self._total * (1 - percent / 100)

    def apply_tax(self) -> None:
        # Modify object's own data
        self._total = self._total * 1.18

    def validate(self) -> None:
        # Validation logic here
        pass

    def get_total(self) -> float:
        return self._total


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Create order object
    order = Order(1000)

    # Object performs actions on itself
    order.validate()

    # Tax applied
    order.apply_tax()

    # Discount applied
    order.apply_discount(10)

    print(order.get_total())

blocks.content: NOTICE THE KEY DIFFERENCE

The functional version never mutates the original order it returns a brand new one. The OOP version modifies this.total directly. Neither is wrong they're just different philosophies about how state should be managed.
4. Strengths and weaknesses of each

Both paradigms have trade-offs. Functional design excels at predictability and scalability, while object-oriented design is better for modelling complex real-world systems and organizing large codebases.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512621823-927475625.png
blocks.alt: Diagram mapping the main strengths of each paradigm, predictability and safe concurrency for functional design against modelling real entities and scaling across teams for object oriented design

blocks.content: Functional Design

["Predictability. Pure functions always return the same output for the same input. No hidden state, no surprises. This makes debugging dramatically easier you can test each function in total isolation.
","Concurrency. Immutable data means no two threads can corrupt shared state. Functional code scales to parallel execution naturally no locks, no race conditions.
","Where it struggles. When you're modelling things that naturally have identity and changing state over time a user's account, an ongoing order, a game character functional code gets awkward. You end up threading state manually through every function."]
items: Predictability. Pure functions always return the same output for the same input. No hidden state, no surprises. This makes debugging dramatically easier you can test each function in total isolation.
Concurrency. Immutable data means no two threads can corrupt shared state. Functional code scales to parallel execution naturally no locks, no race conditions.

Where it struggles. When you're modelling things that naturally have identity and changing state over time a user's account, an ongoing order, a game character functional code gets awkward. You end up threading state manually through every function.

blocks.content: Object-Oriented Design

["Modelling reality. The real world has entities customers, orders, drivers, payments and OOP maps directly to these concepts. It makes large complex systems easier to reason about at a human level.
","Team scale. Clear class boundaries mean large teams can work on different parts of the same system without constant collisions. Interfaces create contracts between teams, not just between classes.
","Where it struggles. When overused, OOP creates unnecessary complexity. Forcing everything into a class even simple data transformations adds boilerplate without benefit. Mutable shared state also makes concurrency tricky.

blocks.content: 5. What you need to know In LLD interviews
blocks.text: 5. What you need to know In LLD interviews

blocks.content: LLD interviews are almost always OOP-focused. Companies ask you to design classes, define relationships, apply patterns all of which are OOP concepts. But knowing functional ideas makes your OOP design better.

["WHAT Functional Design TEACHES YOUR OOP
"]
items: WHAT Functional Design TEACHES YOUR OOP

blocks.content: Keep methods small and side-effect-free wherever possible. A method that only reads and returns is easier to test than one that modifies state. Immutability where it makes sense reduces bugs drastically.

["WHAT OOP DOES THAT Functional Design CAN'T EASILY
"]
items: WHAT OOP DOES THAT Functional Design CAN'T EASILY

blocks.content: Model systems where entities have identity, lifecycle, and evolving state. An Order that goes from PLACED to DELIVERED is naturally an object not a series of pure functions.

THE MODERN REALITY: Most production systems blend both. Java and Python classes with functional-style helper methods. React components (OOP-ish) using hooks that borrow from functional thinking. The best engineers reach for whichever tool fits the problem not the one they know best.
6. Worked example, calculating a shopping cart total
blocks.text: 6. Worked example, calculating a shopping cart total

blocks.content: A shopping cart total is a small enough problem to hold in your head, yet it touches everything that matters here: a list of items, a discount, a tax rate, and one final number. Solving it both ways makes the contrast between the two paradigms concrete instead of abstract.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512623476-391178813.png
blocks.alt: Diagram contrasting the shopping cart worked example, a functional pipeline turning the items list into a total versus an object accumulating state through addItem, applyDiscount and applyTax calls

blocks.content: THE PROBLEM

Given a list of cart items, each with a price and a quantity, calculate the final total after applying a discount percentage and then a tax percentage. Simple on paper, but the two paradigms reach for completely different building blocks to solve it.
FUNCTIONAL APPROACH
There is no cart object here at all, only plain data and a chain of pure functions. Each function takes a number in, returns a new number out, and never touches anything outside its own arguments.
Notice that the cart itself is just a list, and the total emerges from composing small functions together, subtotal, then discount, then tax. Nothing anywhere holds on to intermediate state.
OBJECT-ORIENTED APPROACH
Here the cart is a real object. It owns its list of items and its own discount and tax settings, and it knows how to compute its own total on request.
The state lives inside the ShoppingCart instance between calls. You build it up step by step, addItem, applyDiscount, applyTax, and getTotal reads whatever the object currently holds.
WHAT CHANGED BETWEEN THE TWO

The functional version never creates a cart object at all, the cart is just an array and the total is the return value of one function call with three inputs. The OOP version keeps a long lived cart that accumulates items and settings over multiple calls, and the total depends on whatever mutations have happened to it so far. Both arrive at the same number, they just disagree about where that number should live in between steps.

{"headers":["Aspect","Functional cart","OOP cart"],"rows":[["Where the total lives","Nowhere until computed, it is the return value of a function","Inside the cart object, recomputed on demand from its own fields"],["How discount and tax are tracked","Passed as plain arguments through the pipeline","Stored as fields on the cart, set once and reused across calls"],["Adding a new item","Build a new list, the original list is untouched","Call addItem, the same cart object grows in place"],["Extending with a coupon rule","Add one more pure function to the pipeline","Add one more method or field to ShoppingCart"],["Safety under concurrent access","Safe by default, nothing is shared or mutated","Needs explicit synchronisation if two threads touch the same cart"]]}
TESTING THE TWO VERSIONS

This is where the functional style shows its biggest practical advantage. Testing cartTotal means calling it with a hardcoded list and two numbers, then asserting on the return value, there is nothing to set up and nothing to tear down. Testing ShoppingCart means constructing an instance, calling addItem twice, calling applyDiscount, calling applyTax, and only then asserting on getTotal, the test has to recreate the exact sequence of state changes a real caller would perform.

blocks.title: A quick mental test
blocks.text: If you can describe the correct behaviour of a piece of logic using only the words input and output, a pure function will probably be simpler to write and test. If your description needs the words before and after, or first and then, you are describing state changes, and an object is probably the more natural fit.

blocks.content: 7. Choosing between them, and why most real systems mix both
blocks.text: 7. Choosing between them, and why most real systems mix both

blocks.content: Neither paradigm wins outright. The honest answer, the one that actually holds up in production codebases, is that most systems use both at once, just in different layers.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512625394-354070405.png
blocks.alt: Decision diagram for choosing a paradigm based on whether you are building a data pipeline or calculation versus modelling an entity with identity and lifecycle

blocks.content: WHEN FUNCTIONAL DESIGN WINS

["Data pipelines and ETL jobs, where the whole job is a series of transformations applied to records.","Calculating derived values from inputs that never change once they arrive, pricing, totals, aggregates, and reports.","Anything that needs to run safely across multiple threads or machines at once, since immutable data cannot be corrupted by concurrent access.","Code where correctness and testability matter more than anything else, since pure functions are the easiest kind of code to prove correct."]
items: Data pipelines and ETL jobs, where the whole job is a series of transformations applied to records.
Calculating derived values from inputs that never change once they arrive, pricing, totals, aggregates, and reports.
Anything that needs to run safely across multiple threads or machines at once, since immutable data cannot be corrupted by concurrent access.
Code where correctness and testability matter more than anything else, since pure functions are the easiest kind of code to prove correct.

blocks.content: These are all situations where there is no meaningful identity to track, only values flowing through a chain of steps.
WHEN OBJECT-ORIENTED DESIGN WINS

["Entities with a real lifecycle, an order that moves from placed to shipped to delivered, a user session that opens and eventually closes.","Systems with a lot of shared state that many parts of the codebase need to read and update consistently, an inventory count, a bank balance.","Large codebases built by large teams, where class boundaries and interfaces let different groups work independently without stepping on each other.","Domains that map naturally onto real world nouns, customers, drivers, vehicles, rooms, where thinking in objects matches how humans already think about the problem."]
items: Entities with a real lifecycle, an order that moves from placed to shipped to delivered, a user session that opens and eventually closes.
Systems with a lot of shared state that many parts of the codebase need to read and update consistently, an inventory count, a bank balance.
Large codebases built by large teams, where class boundaries and interfaces let different groups work independently without stepping on each other.
Domains that map naturally onto real world nouns, customers, drivers, vehicles, rooms, where thinking in objects matches how humans already think about the problem.

blocks.content: THE HYBRID PATTERN, FUNCTIONAL CORE, IMPERATIVE SHELL
blocks.text: THE HYBRID PATTERN, FUNCTIONAL CORE, IMPERATIVE SHELL

blocks.content: This is the pattern most mature codebases converge on whether or not anyone names it explicitly. The core business rules, pricing, discount calculations, validation, are written as small pure functions with no side effects. A thin shell of stateful objects sits around that core and handles everything the core deliberately avoids, database reads and writes, network calls, tracking what has already happened. The shell calls the pure core, the core never calls back into the shell.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512627070-843114008.png
blocks.alt: Diagram of the functional core, imperative shell hybrid pattern, the shell handles input and output while a pure functional core sits in the middle

blocks.content: ["React function components paired with hooks, the rendering logic is a pure function of props and state, while hooks manage the messier stateful parts underneath.","Redux and similar state containers, reducers are pure functions, but the store itself is a stateful object that holds the current state between dispatches.","Java services that use the Streams API for calculations inside otherwise ordinary stateful classes and repositories.","Python codebases that pair small stateless module level functions for calculations with classes and dataclasses for anything that needs identity or persistence."]
items: React function components paired with hooks, the rendering logic is a pure function of props and state, while hooks manage the messier stateful parts underneath.
Redux and similar state containers, reducers are pure functions, but the store itself is a stateful object that holds the current state between dispatches.
Java services that use the Streams API for calculations inside otherwise ordinary stateful classes and repositories.
Python codebases that pair small stateless module level functions for calculations with classes and dataclasses for anything that needs identity or persistence.

blocks.content: Keep the core pure and the shell thin. Most bugs live in the shell, not the core, so the smaller you can make the shell, the fewer places bugs have to hide.

{"pros":["Business rules stay pure and easy to test, even while the surrounding system is full of state, databases, and network calls.","Teams can review and reason about the calculation logic in isolation, separate from the messier stateful classes that invoke it.","Adoption can be incremental, a team can introduce pure functions inside an existing OOP codebase one method at a time, without a rewrite."],"cons":["Mixing styles without a shared convention creates inconsistency, some classes are pure, some are not, and new engineers cannot tell which is which just by reading the class name.","Over applying functional purity inside a language and team that thinks in mutation adds ceremony, wrapper types and extra copying, for no real benefit.","It requires discipline, the team needs an explicit rule for which layer owns state and which layer must stay pure, otherwise the codebase slowly drifts back into a mutable mess."]}
HONEST GUIDANCE

Nobody ships a large production system built entirely in one paradigm. The backend that processes payments almost certainly has objects representing accounts and transactions, and pure functions computing interest, fees, and totals inside them. Treat functional and object-oriented design as tools in the same toolbox, not as a religion you have to pick a side in. Reach for a pure function when the question is what does this produce, and reach for an object when the question is what is this and what can it become over time.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.content: If you find yourself asking what does this do, given these inputs, reach for a function. If you find yourself asking what is this, and what can it become, reach for an object. Most real features need a bit of both, and that is fine.

Back in an LLD interview, this is worth saying out loud if it comes up: your class diagram will be OOP, and it should be, but the methods inside those classes are free to be small, pure, and side-effect-free wherever the logic allows it. That combination, OOP structure with functional discipline inside it, is usually what separates a design that merely works from one that is easy to extend and easy to test.
